Co-existing health needs in transgender and gender diverse populations: extracted data from the included studies

Supplementary data for the integrative review by Kearns, Abdul Wahab, Gardner, Kontonika, McCarthy, White and Neff (Issues in Mental Health Nursing, under review). 182 studies are included; a study appears under every health domain for which it reported findings, so the four tables together hold 375 entries.

Search by author, year, design, population or any word in the findings. Click a column heading to sort. Open a row to read the extracted findings and the full reference; "Source" opens the paper at its DOI.

Key Findings

•Self-rated mental health: Fair or poor mental health was reported by 68.0% of diagnosed autistic and 72.4% of self-identified autistic TNB participants, compared with 53.1% of allistic participants. •Mental health disparity (adjusted): Compared with allistic participants, self-identified autistic individuals had substantially higher odds of reporting fair or poor mental health (AOR 5.73), while diagnosed autistic participants also had elevated odds (AOR 1.79). •Unmet mental health needs: Unmet health care needs (including mental health care) were reported by 54.8% of diagnosed autistic and 60.9% of self-identified autistic participants, compared with 42.6% of allistic participants. •Negative mental health care experiences: Autistic participants more frequently reported negative experiences with mental health providers, including repeated misgendering (≈19–21% vs 13.6%) and providers being unable to separate mental health concerns from TNB identity (≈14–19% vs 11.1%). •Disclosure avoidance during assessments: Among those undergoing mental health or readiness assessments for gender-affirming care, 25.5% of diagnosed and 36.1% of self-identified autistic participants avoided disclosing autism due to concerns about access to care. •Provider knowledge burden: Autistic participants more often reported needing to educate mental health providers about TNB-related needs (25.9% diagnosed; 40.0% self-identified vs 26.8% allistic). •Overall mental health pattern: Autistic transgender and nonbinary individuals experienced significantly poorer self-rated mental health, higher unmet mental health needs, and more negative mental health care experiences than allistic peers, with the greatest disparities observed among self-identified autistic individuals.

Reference

Adams, N., Jacobsen, K., Li, L., Francino, M., Rutherford, L., Tei, C., Scheim, A., & Bauer, G. (2025). Health and health care access of autistic transgender and nonbinary people in Canada: A cross-sectional study. Autism in Adulthood, 7(1), 66–80. https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2023.0024

Key Findings

•Suicidal ideation: 19.1% of gender-referred children were rated by parents as talking about killing themselves, compared with 5.8% of siblings and 1.7% of non-referred children. •Self-harm / suicide attempts: 6.5% of gender-referred children were rated as deliberately self-harming or attempting suicide, compared with 2.2% of siblings and 0.2% of non-referred children. •Age effects: Suicidal ideation increased with age; by ages 10–12 years, approximately 30% of gender-referred children were rated as expressing suicidal ideation. •Comparative risk: After adjustment for age, gender-referred children were 5.1 times more likely than non-referred children to talk about suicide and 8.6 times more likely to self-harm or attempt suicide. •Behavioural correlates: General behavioural and emotional problems were strongly associated with suicidality; controlling for these reduced but did not eliminate elevated risk. •Peer relations: Poor peer relationships were associated with suicidality, but this association was no longer significant after accounting for overall behavioural problems. •Sibling risk: Siblings of gender-referred children also showed elevated risk, being 2.7–3.6 times more likely than non-referred children to show suicidal ideation or self-harm. •Overall pattern: A sizeable minority of gender-referred children demonstrated clinically significant suicidality, particularly in later childhood, supporting the need for routine screening and comprehensive mental health assessment.

Reference

Aitken, M., VanderLaan, D. P., Wasserman, L., Stojanovski, S., & Zucker, K. J. (2016). Self-harm and suicidality in children referred for gender dysphoria. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 55(6), 513–520. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaac.2016.04.001

Key Findings

•Any suicidal ideation: 100% of participants scored above zero on the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation. •Low-risk suicidal ideation: 19.1% were classified as low risk. •High-risk suicidal ideation: 71.4% were classified as high risk. •Very high-risk suicidal ideation: 9.5% were classified as very high risk. •Age effects: Higher age was associated with greater severity of suicidal ideation. •Education effects: Higher educational attainment was associated with higher suicidal ideation scores. •Overall pattern: Suicidal ideation severity was extremely high, even in a sample without psychiatric comorbidity, indicating substantial baseline suicide risk in individuals seeking legal confirmation of gender transition.

Key Findings

•Ever thought about suicide: 70.3% of transgender and 77.9% of non-binary youth reported suicidal ideation, compared with 40.6% of cisgender youth. •Psychological distress (GHQ-12): 52.3% of transgender and 55.7% of non-binary youth screened positive for psychological health problems, compared with 38.4% of cisgender youth. •Feeling isolated: 40.3% of transgender and 54.3% of non-binary youth reported feeling isolated, compared with 29.0% of cisgender youth. •Happiness: Only 66.1% of transgender and 61.4% of non-binary youth reported being happy or very happy, compared with 83.5% of cisgender youth. •Self-harm–related vulnerability: Elevated psychological distress and suicidality were most pronounced among non-binary youth. •Overall pattern: Transgender and non-binary young people showed substantially higher psychological distress, social isolation, and suicidal ideation than cisgender peers, with non-binary youth consistently the most affected.

Key Findings

•Suicide mortality: Transfeminine participants had a significantly elevated suicide risk, with a standardised mortality ratio (SMR) of 5.70, indicating nearly six times higher suicide mortality compared with the general population. •External causes linked to mental health: Deaths due to suicide and illicit drug use contributed substantially to excess mortality; deaths from external causes were almost eightfold higher than expected. •Timing of suicides: No suicides occurred within the first two years of hormone treatment; suicides occurred after longer treatment durations (2–5 years, 5–10 years, and >10 years). •Psychiatric history: 76% of those who died by suicide had received psychiatric treatment prior to death, suggesting pre-existing or ongoing mental health needs. •Hormone treatment and suicide: No association was found between current cyproterone acetate use and suicide risk. •Transmasculine participants: No statistically significant increase in suicide or overall mental-health–related mortality was observed in transmasculine participants compared with the general population.

Reference

Asscheman, H., Giltay, E. J., Megens, J. A., de Ronde, W. P., van Trotsenburg, M. A., & Gooren, L. J. (2011). A long-term follow-up study of mortality in transsexuals receiving treatment with cross-sex hormones. European Journal of Endocrinology, 164(4), 635–642. https://doi.org/10.1530/EJE-10-1038

Key Findings

•Overall psychopathological burden: 100% of transsexual participants reported significantly higher psychopathological symptom levels across all SCL-90-R subscales compared with healthy controls (all p < .001). •Depressive symptoms (SCL-90-R): Mean depression scores were significantly higher in transfeminine participants (0.85) compared with transmasculine participants (0.45) (p = .001), representing a medium effect size. •Anxiety and phobic anxiety: Transsexual participants reported significantly elevated anxiety and phobic anxiety symptoms compared with controls (all p < .001), with stronger sex effects observed when compared to phenotypic-sex–matched controls. •Paranoid ideation and interpersonal sensitivity: Significantly higher scores were observed across these domains in transsexual participants compared with healthy controls (all p < .001). •Global psychological distress (GSI): Overall psychological distress was significantly elevated in transsexual participants compared with controls (all p < .001), with transfeminine participants showing the highest mean GSI scores. •Clinical depression diagnosis: A documented lifetime diagnosis of depression was reported by 13.5% of transfeminine and 15.6% of transmasculine participants, with no significant difference between groups. •Psychopathological profile similarity: Transmasculine participants’ symptom profiles most closely resembled phenotypic male controls (r = .945), while transfeminine participants showed slightly greater similarity to phenotypic female controls (r = .698) than genetic-sex controls. •Overall pattern: Transsexual participants demonstrated a broad elevation in psychological distress, with depressive symptoms most pronounced among transfeminine individuals, supporting phenotypic-sex–matched controls as the most appropriate comparison group.

Reference

Auer, M. K., Hohne, N., Bazarra-Castro, M. A., Pfister, H., Fuss, J., Stalla, G. K., Sievers, C., & Ising, M. (2013). Psychopathological profiles in transsexuals and the challenge of their special status among the sexes. PLOS ONE, 8(10), Article e78469. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0078469

Key Findings

•Suicidal ideation (lifetime): 84% of respondents reported having thought about ending their life. •Recent suicidal ideation: 63% reported suicidal thoughts in the past year, 27% in the past week, and 4% daily. •Suicide attempts (lifetime): 35% of the total sample reported at least one suicide attempt. •Repeated suicide attempts: 25% reported more than one suicide attempt; 3% reported more than ten attempts. •Recent suicide attempts: 11% reported a suicide attempt within the past year. •Current suicide planning: 3.2% reported actively planning to attempt suicide; 11% were unsure about near-future intent. •Comparative risk: Trans participants were estimated to be up to seven times more likely to attempt suicide than the general population. •Impact of transition: 67% reported suicidal thoughts were more frequent before transition, compared with 3% reporting increased suicidality after transition. •Overall pattern: Very high levels of suicidality were observed, with marked reductions following social and/or medical transition.

Reference

Bailey, L., Ellis, S. J., & McNeil, J. (2014). Suicide risk in the UK trans population and the role of gender transition in decreasing suicidal ideation and suicide attempt. Mental Health Review Journal, 19(4), 209–220. https://doi.org/10.1108/mhrj-05-2014-0015

Key Findings

•Suicidal ideation (past year): 35.1% of transgender participants reported serious consideration of suicide in the past year. •Suicide attempts (past year): 11.2% reported at least one suicide attempt in the past year. •Social support: High overall social support (90th vs 10th percentile) was associated with a 49% reduction in suicide ideation (RR 0.51) and an 82% reduction in attempts among those with ideation (RR 0.18). •Parental support: Strong parental support for gender identity was associated with reduced suicide ideation (RR 0.43), corresponding to a potential prevention of 17% of ideation cases at the population level. •Transphobia: Lower transphobia exposure (10th vs 90th percentile) was associated with a 66% reduction in suicide ideation (RR 0.34) and a further 76% reduction in suicide attempts among those with ideation (RR 0.24). •Identity document concordance: Having at least one identity document concordant with lived gender was associated with reduced suicide ideation (RR 0.56) and attempts (RR 0.26). •Medical transition: Among those who desired medical transition, completion was associated with reduced suicide ideation (RR 0.38); among those with ideation, being “in process” was associated with increased attempt risk (RR 2.91). •Overall mental health pattern: Transgender people experienced very high rates of recent suicidal ideation and attempts; lower suicide risk was strongly associated with modifiable social and structural factors—particularly reduced transphobia, strong parental support, identity document concordance, and access to completed medical transition—highlighting suicide risk as highly sensitive to social and policy environments.

Reference

Bauer, G. R., Scheim, A. I., Pyne, J., Travers, R., & Hammond, R. (2015). Intervenable factors associated with suicide risk in transgender persons: A respondent driven sampling study in Ontario, Canada. BMC Public Health, 15, 525. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-015-1867-2

Key Findings

•Depression (PHQ-9): 35% of participants met criteria for moderately severe to severe depression (PHQ-9 ≥15). •Any depressive symptoms: 65% scored above minimal depression (PHQ-9 ≥10), indicating at least moderate depressive symptoms. •Suicidal ideation (recent): 32–33% reported thoughts of self-harm or that they would be better off dead within the previous two weeks. •Perceived discrimination: 39% experienced discrimination at least weekly (25% once/twice weekly; 14% daily), reflecting high chronic exposure. •Sexual partner violence: 57–60% reported a history of violence or mistreatment by a sexual partner or spouse. •Discrimination–depression association: Higher perceived discrimination was associated with increased odds of moderately severe to severe depression (OR 1.20, p<.01). •Violence–depression association: Sexual partner violence was associated with nearly two-fold higher odds of severe depression (OR 1.91, p<.01). •Overall pattern: Depression and suicidality were highly prevalent in this low-income Latina transfeminine cohort and were strongly associated with discrimination and partner violence.

Reference

Bazargan, M., & Galvan, F. (2012). Perceived discrimination and depression among low-income Latina male-to-female transgender women. BMC Public Health, 12, 663. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2458-12-663

Key Findings

•Overall psychosocial/psychological vulnerability: Adolescents had a mean of 5.6 vulnerability factors (range 0–13); 54% had ≥6 co-occurring vulnerability factors. •Any DSM-IV psychiatric diagnosis: 60% had at least one psychiatric diagnosis other than gender dysphoria. •Multiple psychiatric diagnoses: Among those diagnosed, 64% had two or more DSM diagnoses. •Suicidal ideation: 62% had a documented history of suicidal ideation. •Self-harm: 36% had a history of deliberate self-harm. •Suicide attempts: 26% had made at least one suicide attempt. •Psychiatric treatment history: 78% had received outpatient psychological therapy and 54% had prior or current psychopharmacological treatment. •Clinical-level distress: 60% scored in the clinical range on youth self-report (YSR) and 69% on parent report (CBCL). •Overall pattern: A majority of adolescents presented with substantial psychiatric comorbidity and suicidality, supporting the need for comprehensive mental health assessment beyond gender dysphoria alone.

Reference

Key Findings

•High psychological distress: Participants described pervasive experiences of depression, anxiety, fear, and emotional exhaustion linked to intersecting racism, transphobia, poverty, and social exclusion. •Suicidality and self-harm: Suicidal ideation and suicide attempts were frequently discussed, particularly during periods of housing instability, family rejection, and economic precarity. •Trauma exposure: Narratives highlighted repeated exposure to physical and sexual violence, often associated with survival strategies such as sex work and unsafe living environments. •Substance use as coping: Alcohol and drug use were commonly described as coping mechanisms in response to chronic stress, trauma, and marginalisation. •Barriers to care: Mental health needs were often unmet due to discrimination within healthcare services, lack of insurance, and fear of mistreatment. •Protective factors: Peer support, community connection, and access to culturally competent, affirming services were identified as critical buffers against worsening mental health.

Key Findings

•Anxiety and distress: Participants described heightened anxiety and emotional distress linked to uncertainty, unclear processes, and fear of care being denied or withdrawn. •Gatekeeping-related distress: Many reported suppressing discussion of mental health difficulties due to concern that disclosure would be misinterpreted and used to restrict access to gender-affirming care. •Misdiagnosis and invalidation: Autistic traits were frequently misinterpreted as psychiatric pathology, contributing to distress, delayed care, or service exclusion. •Sensory-related stress: Overstimulating clinical environments and disruption to routines were described as exacerbating anxiety and emotional dysregulation. •Communication burden: Limited communication options and poor responsiveness from services increased stress and feelings of being unsupported. •Structural stressors: Long waiting lists, bureaucratic complexity, and insurance barriers were described as having a sustained negative impact on mental well-being. •Overall pattern: Autistic transgender and non-binary adults reported significant mental health burden driven by structural, sensory, and gatekeeping-related barriers, with distress arising less from gender identity itself and more from how services were organised, delivered, and interpreted autistic embodiment.

Key Findings

Key Findings

•Anxiety and depression: At baseline, median HADS anxiety scores were elevated (overall median 7–9), and depressive symptoms were common (median ~6–7). •Change over time: Depression scores significantly decreased after 1 year of gender-affirming hormone therapy in both transgender men (−1.42 points, p = .019) and transgender women (−1.05 points, p = .013). Key Findings

Key Findings

•Overall psychological functioning: Total psychopathology scores (CBCL/YSR) significantly decreased after GnRHa initiation compared with the pre-treatment assessment phase (p < .01). •Depression: Depressive symptom scores increased during the assessment period but decreased significantly following GnRHa treatment, falling below clinical cut-off levels at follow-up (p < .05). •Anxiety: Anxiety scores significantly decreased after GnRHa initiation (p < .05), with no significant improvement observed during assessment alone. •Suicidality: Scores reflecting suicidal ideation (e.g. “repulsion by life”) improved significantly after treatment initiation (p < .05). •Internalising symptoms: Internalising problems (anxious–depressive symptoms, somatic complaints) reduced significantly following GnRHa treatment (p < .01). •Externalising symptoms: Externalising behaviour scores decreased significantly post-treatment (p < .05). •Body-related psychological distress: Body uneasiness scores increased during assessment but improved significantly after GnRHa treatment (p < .01). •Temporal pattern: Across outcomes, no significant mental health improvements occurred prior to GnRHa, whereas multiple domains improved significantly after treatment initiation.

Key Findings

•Social distress: Mean social anxiety/distress scores (SADS) were in the normal range overall but were significantly higher in untreated patients compared with those receiving cross-sex hormone therapy (F = 4.36, p = .038). •Anxiety symptoms: Clinically relevant anxiety symptoms were reported by 61% of untreated patients versus 33% of hormone-treated patients; mean anxiety scores were significantly lower in treated patients (F = 14.59, p = .001). •Depressive symptoms: Depressive symptoms were reported by 31% of untreated patients compared with 8% of treated patients; mean depression scores were significantly lower among those receiving hormones (F = 9.52, p = .002). •Symptom severity: Across groups, mean anxiety and depression scores were generally subclinical, indicating elevated distress rather than categorical psychiatric disorder. •Treatment status: Length of time on hormone therapy was not correlated with anxiety, depression, or social distress scores, suggesting differences were related to treatment status rather than duration. •Surgical status: Among hormone-treated patients, mental health scores did not differ between those who had and had not undergone gender-affirming surgery. •Overall pattern: Untreated individuals showed consistently higher levels of anxiety, depression, and social distress than those receiving cross-sex hormone therapy.

•Gender identity prevalence: 1.3% identified as transgender and 1.4% as gender questioning; 97.3% identified as cisgender. •Past-year suicidal ideation (adjusted): Gender questioning youth had significantly higher risk of past-year suicidal ideation compared with cisgender youth after full adjustment. •Past-year suicide attempts (adjusted): Transgender youth had significantly higher risk of past-year suicide attempts compared with cisgender youth. •Suicide attempts requiring treatment (adjusted): Transgender youth had significantly higher risk of suicide attempts requiring medical treatment. •Victimisation exposure: Gender minority youth experienced higher rates of school and dating-related victimisation than cisgender peers. •Sadness/hopelessness: Gender minority youth were more likely to report persistent sadness or hopelessness. •Substance use: Transgender youth reported higher recent use of tobacco, alcohol, and marijuana. •Adjusted models: Elevated suicide risk among gender minority youth persisted after controlling for victimisation, sadness/hopelessness, and substance use. •Overall pattern: Gender minority youth represented a small proportion of the population but experienced disproportionately elevated suicide risk, particularly for suicide attempts and attempts requiring treatment.

Jackman, K. B., Caceres, B. A., Kreuze, E. J., & Bockting, W. O. (2021). Suicidality among gender minority youth: Analysis of 2017 Youth Risk Behavior Survey data. Archives of Suicide Research, 25(2), 208–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/13811118.2019.1678539

Key Findings

•Overall mortality linked to mental health–related causes: Transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) adults had higher overall mortality than cisgender comparators, with 34–75% increased risk, largely driven by deaths from external causes, including suicide and accidental poisoning. •Suicide and homicide: TGD individuals were 3.34 times more likely to die from suicide or homicide than cisgender men (MRR 3.34, 95% CI 1.70–6.54) and 5.62 times more likely than cisgender women (MRR 5.62, 95% CI 2.65–11.91). •Accidental poisoning: Mortality from accidental poisonings was elevated, with TGD individuals 2.28 times higher than cisgender men and 5.20 times higher than cisgender women, suggesting overlap with substance-related and mental health vulnerabilities. •Sex-specific patterns: Transfeminine adults showed higher mortality from external causes compared with cisgender women (MRR 1.92), while transmasculine adults had an even higher relative risk (MRR 2.77 vs cisgender women). •Mental and behavioural disorder mortality: Deaths coded under mental and behavioural disorders were uncommon and not significantly elevated, indicating excess mental health burden is reflected primarily through external causes rather than psychiatric diagnoses on death certificates. •Highest-risk subgroup: TGD individuals with unknown sex assigned at birth (including many non-binary people) had the highest mortality risk, suggesting heightened vulnerability linked to marginalisation and unmet mental health needs. •Interpretive framing: Authors attribute excess suicide and external-cause mortality to minority stress, discrimination, and social exclusion, rather than intrinsic psychopathology.

Reference

Jackson, S. S., Brown, J., Pfeiffer, R. M., Shrewsbury, D., O’Callaghan, S., Berner, A. M., Gadalla, S. M., & Shiels, M. S. (2023). Analysis of mortality among transgender and gender diverse adults in England. JAMA Network Open, 6(1), Article e2253687. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.53687

•Past-year suicidal ideation: 56.6% reported suicidal ideation in the past year. •Lifetime suicide plans or attempts: 66.0% reported a lifetime history of suicide plans and/or attempts. •Lifetime suicide plans: 34.0% reported having made a suicide plan. •Lifetime suicide attempts: 32.0% reported at least one suicide attempt. •History of homelessness: 33.5% reported a history of homelessness. •Employment discrimination: 34.0% reported employment discrimination related to transgender identity. •Housing discrimination: 11.8% reported housing discrimination. •Military enacted stigma: 29.2% reported stigma or punishment related to gender identity during military service. •Mental health correlates: Suicidality was strongly associated with depressive symptoms and PTSD symptoms. •Key risk factors: History of homelessness and military felt stigma showed the strongest associations with suicidality. •Overall pattern: Transgender veterans experienced very high levels of suicidality, strongly patterned by mental health burden, stigma during military service, and socioeconomic vulnerability.

Reference

Lehavot, K., Simpson, T. L., & Shipherd, J. C. (2016). Factors associated with suicidality among a national sample of transgender veterans. Suicide and Life-Threatening Behavior, 46(5), 507–524. https://doi.org/10.1111/sltb.12233

Key Findings

•Overall psychiatric morbidity: Psychiatric disease was present in 56.2% of patients, indicating a high burden of mental health comorbidity among individuals seeking hormone therapy. •Mood disorders: Mood disorders (including depression, dysthymia, adjustment disorder, and mania) were the most common psychiatric conditions, affecting 44% of the cohort. •Age-related patterning: Psychiatric morbidity was inversely correlated with age at presentation; mood disorders were less prevalent in those initiating hormone therapy before age 32 (36.3%) compared with those initiating after age 32 (51.7%, p = .011). •Disability and employment: 17% were on disability, with the majority attributed to mental health conditions, and 28% were unemployed or on disability overall. •Substance use: Drug or substance abuse was reported in 11% of patients, more commonly among transfeminine individuals. •Mental health and treatment progression: Among transfeminine patients, the presence of mood disorders was associated with significantly longer time to gender-affirming surgery, suggesting mental health burden may delay care pathways. •Overall pattern: Mental health difficulties—particularly mood disorders—were common and appeared to interact with social functioning, employment, and access to surgical care, supporting the importance of early and integrated mental health support.

Reference

Key Findings

Key Findings

Key Findings

•Depressive symptoms: Depression scores remained stable and largely non-clinical over 24 months; 72% were in the average range at baseline and 71% at follow-up, with no significant worsening over time. •Suicidality: Suicidal ideation decreased from 12% at baseline (11/94) to 8% at 24 months (5/59); suicide plans reduced from three cases to none, and attempts decreased from two to one. •Emotional health: No significant changes were observed across emotional health domains (e.g. loneliness, rejection, self-efficacy), with mean scores remaining below clinical concern thresholds. •Behavioural and emotional problems: Parent-reported internalising and externalising problems remained stable and below clinical cut-offs; a small but significant reduction in rule-breaking behaviour was observed. •Age effects: Older baseline age was associated with higher baseline depression and internalising symptoms, but did not predict worsening mental health trajectories. •Overall mental health pattern: Over 24 months, youth receiving puberty suppression showed stable mental health with low and non-worsening rates of depression, suicidality, and behavioural problems, suggesting prevention of mental health deterioration over time.

Reference

Key Findings

Key Findings

•Depressive symptoms (overall levels): Across all waves, participants reported mild depressive symptoms on average (mean BDI-Y score 13.6), remaining broadly stable over time. •Gender identity variability: 18.3% of youths reported a change in gender identity over approximately 3.5 years; frequency of gender identity variability was not associated with levels of depressive symptoms (β = 2.43, p = .33) or within-person changes in depression over time (β = 0.23, p = .75). •Baseline group differences: Youths transitioning from cisgender to TGD reported higher depressive symptoms at baseline compared with consistently cisgender youths (β = 4.66, p = .03), but this difference was no longer significant after adjusting for exposure to LGBT violence (β = 3.31, p = .16). •Trajectories over time: No gender identity trajectory group differed in the rate of change of depressive symptoms across follow-up; depressive symptom trajectories were stable across all groups. •Role of victimisation: Cumulative exposure to LGBT violence was significantly associated with higher depressive symptoms over time (β = 2.59, p < .001), accounting for observed group differences. •Overall mental health pattern: Changes or variability in gender identity were not associated with worsening depressive symptoms over time; observed differences in depression were largely explained by exposure to LGBT-related violence rather than gender identity trajectories themselves.

Reference

Key Findings

•All-cause mortality: All-cause mortality did not significantly differ between gender-referred adolescents and matched controls (0.5% vs 0.3%); rates were 0.81 vs 0.40 per 1,000 person-years. •Suicide mortality (unadjusted): Suicide deaths were more frequent among gender-referred adolescents than controls (0.3% vs 0.1%); suicide mortality rates were 0.51 vs 0.12 per 1,000 person-years. •Suicide mortality (adjusted for psychiatric morbidity): After adjusting for specialist-level psychiatric treatment, suicide mortality no longer differed between groups (HR 1.8, 95% CI 0.6–4.8). •Role of psychiatric morbidity: Increasing intensity of specialist psychiatric care strongly predicted suicide mortality, with highest risk among those with ≥101 psychiatric contacts (HR 11.1). •Sex differences: Male registered sex was associated with higher suicide mortality risk (adjusted HR 3.8). •Impact of gender-affirming treatment: Suicide mortality did not differ between those who proceeded to gender-affirming treatment and those who did not once psychiatric morbidity was accounted for (GR+ HR 0.8; GR− HR 3.2; both non-significant vs controls). •Overall mental health pattern: Suicide mortality among gender-referred adolescents was rare and, once psychiatric morbidity was accounted for, did not differ from the general population; psychiatric morbidity—not gender dysphoria or gender-affirming treatment—was the primary predictor of suicide risk.

Reference

Ruuska, S. M., Tuisku, K., Holttinen, T., & Kaltiala, R. (2024). All-cause and suicide mortalities among adolescents and young adults who contacted specialised gender identity services in Finland in 1996-2019: A register study. BMJ Mental Health, 27(1). https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2023-300940

Key Findings

•Mental health functioning: Mental health–related quality of life was substantially reduced, with a mean SF-12 mental health score of 32.6 (SD 8.3), almost 2 standard deviations below population norms. •Comparison with non-veterans: Poor mental health functioning was also observed among non-veteran transgender participants (mean 34.6, SD 8.1), indicating distress was not specific to veteran status. •Mental health service use: 34.9% of transgender veterans accessed mental health services in the past year (VA 9.3%, non-VA 25.6%). •Conditions treated: Mental health care addressed gender identity counselling, depression, PTSD, anxiety, relationship difficulties, sleep problems, and grief/bereavement. •Depression: Treatment for depression was reported by 11.7% of transgender veterans (VA 4.7%, non-VA 7.0%). •PTSD: 4.7% received treatment for PTSD, exclusively within VA services. •Barriers to mental health care: Fewer barriers were reported for mental health care than medical care; concerns about provider reactions to gender identity or sexual orientation were endorsed by ~7%. •Overall pattern: Markedly reduced mental health functioning and moderate mental health service use suggest substantial unmet psychological needs, likely influenced by stigma, discrimination, and trauma exposure rather than veteran status alone.

Reference

Shipherd, J. C., Mizock, L., Maguen, S., & Green, K. E. (2012). Male-to-female transgender veterans and VA health care utilization. International Journal of Sexual Health, 24(1), 78–87. https://doi.org/10.1080/19317611.2011.639440

Key Findings

•Prevalence of ASD: 22.5% of trans and gender-diverse young people reported a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. •Psychiatric diagnoses: Trans young people with ASD were significantly more likely to report prior psychiatric diagnoses than those without ASD, including depression (OR 4.87), anxiety disorders (OR 8.00), PTSD (OR 7.97), personality disorders (OR 10.96), psychosis (OR 16.89), eating disorders (OR 6.82), and substance use disorders (OR 12.67). •Current depressive symptoms: Moderate to moderately severe depressive symptoms were more common in the ASD-diagnosed group (OR 1.47). •Current anxiety symptoms: Severe anxiety symptoms were more prevalent among those with ASD (OR 2.18). •Self-harm behaviours: Lifetime self-harm was more frequently reported in the ASD-diagnosed group (OR 1.74). •Suicidal ideation: Lifetime suicidal thoughts were more common among trans youth with ASD (OR 1.72). •Suicide attempts: Lifetime suicide attempts were reported more frequently by the ASD-diagnosed group (OR 1.66). •Risk-taking behaviours: Reckless behaviours intended to put life at risk were more prevalent among those with ASD (OR 1.89). •Overall mental health pattern: Trans and gender-diverse young people with co-occurring ASD experienced substantially higher mental health burden, including elevated psychiatric diagnoses, anxiety, depression, self-harm, and suicidality, compared with their non-ASD peers.

Key Findings

•Internalising problems (pre-treatment): Transgender adolescents at referral showed higher internalising problems than cisgender peers (mean 11.67 vs 9.71; d = 0.24), with 31.3% scoring in the clinical range compared with 22.9% of cisgender adolescents. •Self-harm and suicidality (pre-treatment): Suicidality was more frequently endorsed among adolescents at referral (27.2%) compared with cisgender peers (11.9%). •Peer relation difficulties (pre-treatment): Adolescents at referral reported poorer peer relations than cisgender peers (mean 1.08 vs 0.41; d = 0.62). •Internalising problems (puberty suppression): Adolescents receiving puberty suppression had lower internalising scores than those at referral (mean 7.76 vs 11.67; d = 0.52) and a lower clinical-range prevalence (16.3%). •Self-harm and suicidality (puberty suppression): Suicidality rates among adolescents receiving puberty suppression (12.4%) were similar to cisgender peers (11.9%) and lower than those at referral. •Externalising problems: No significant differences in externalising problems were observed between groups; clinical-range externalising scores were comparable across transgender and cisgender adolescents. •Comparison with cisgender peers (post-treatment): Adolescents receiving puberty suppression showed similar or fewer emotional and behavioural problems compared with cisgender adolescents on internalising and suicidality measures. •Overall mental health pattern: Transgender adolescents demonstrated elevated internalising problems, suicidality, and peer difficulties prior to treatment; following initiation of gender-affirmative care involving puberty suppression, mental health outcomes were comparable to or better than those of cisgender peers from the general population.

Key Findings

•Depressive symptoms (PHQ-9): Depression severity was high overall in this TNB young adult sample, but prevalence at diagnostic thresholds was not reported. •Community connectedness: Community connectedness was not directly associated with depressive symptom severity. •Gender rumination: Higher gender-related rumination was strongly associated with greater depressive symptoms. •Preoccupation with others’ perceptions: This was strongly associated with depression and mediated 35.9% of the relationship between community connectedness and depression. •Gender reflection: Gender reflection showed a weak positive association with depression in bivariate analyses and was not a significant mediator in multivariable models. •Overall pattern: Depression among TNB young adults appeared to be driven less by community connectedness itself and more by maladaptive self-focused attention, particularly rumination and hypervigilance about others’ perceptions.

•Adults with ≥2 clinical-range MMPI scales: 62.8% of adults scored in the clinical range on two or more MMPI clinical scales. •Adults with ≥4 clinical-range scales: 35.5% of adults scored in the clinical range on four or more clinical scales. •Adolescents with ≤1 clinical-range scale: 67.5% of adolescents scored in the clinical range on none or only one MMPI scale. •Adolescents with ≥4 clinical-range scales: 16.9% of adolescents scored in the clinical range on four or more scales. •Adult paranoia (clinical range): 49.8% of adults scored in the clinical range for paranoia, compared with 18.1% of adolescents. •Adult psychasthenia (clinical range): 36.9% of adults scored in the clinical range for psychasthenia, compared with 13.3% of adolescents. •Adult depression (clinical range, MtF): 31.4% of transfeminine adults scored in the clinical range for depression. •Adult depression (clinical range, FtM): 19.8% of transmasculine adults scored in the clinical range for depression. •Overall pattern: Adults with gender identity disorder demonstrated a substantially higher burden of clinically significant psychological distress than adolescents, with over one-third exhibiting multi-domain psychopathology, while the majority of adolescents showed minimal or no clinical-range psychological dysfunction.

Key Findings

Extracted findings

Population

Adults

Age range (years)

18–46

Key findings

This thematic analysis identified multiple structural and professional barriers affecting autistic gender-diverse individuals’ access to gender-affirming healthcare. Key challenges included limited professional knowledge of autism and gender-diverse healthcare needs, inadequate communication methods and accommodations, and misattribution or misdiagnosis of mental health difficulties. Participants also reported significant accessibility barriers, such as unmet sensory needs, disruption to routines, lack of local services, and prolonged waiting times. Bureaucratic and economic obstacles—including unclear care pathways, rigid standardisation of services, and complex or inaccessible insurance processes—further impeded access to care. Participants emphasised the importance of incorporating service-user perspectives to improve the accessibility and quality of gender-affirming healthcare.

Reference

• General health: Autistic participants reported significantly worse self-rated physical health than allistic peers (higher odds of “fair/poor” health in both diagnosed and self-identified groups). • Unmet healthcare needs: 54.8% (diagnosed) and 60.9% (self-identified) reported unmet healthcare needs vs 42.6% of allistic participants (adjusted ORs 1.50–1.79). • Primary care access: No significant difference in having a primary care provider, but greater barriers to effective care among autistic participants. • Healthcare access barriers: Greater difficulty affording care and higher likelihood of care avoidance due to anticipated discrimination.

Overall findings / implications

• Autistic TNB individuals experience poorer physical health status and greater unmet healthcare needs than allistic TNB peers. • Health inequities appear driven by access barriers, stigma, and structural exclusion rather than disease-specific burden alone. • Findings support the need for accessible, autism-affirming, and integrated physical healthcare models. • Highlights the importance of needs-based service access rather than diagnosis-restricted eligibility models.

Reference

Adams, N., Jacobsen, K., Li, L., Francino, M., Rutherford, L., Tei, C., Scheim, A., & Bauer, G. (2025). Health and health care access of autistic transgender and nonbinary people in Canada: A cross-sectional study. Autism in Adulthood, 7(1), 66–80. https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2023.0024

Physical health findings

• Myocardial infarction (self-reported): Higher prevalence among transgender adults compared with cisgender comparators. • Adjusted odds: – Transgender men: >2-fold higher odds of MI vs cisgender men (OR 2.53, 95% CI 1.14–5.63) and ~5-fold vs cisgender women (OR 4.90, 95% CI 2.21–10.90). – Transgender women: >2-fold higher odds vs cisgender women (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.78–3.68); no significant difference vs cisgender men after adjustment. • Cardiovascular risk factors: Higher prevalence of smoking, lower physical activity, and comparable rates of hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia, and kidney disease relative to cisgender groups. • Age: Transgender respondents were younger on average than cisgender comparators, yet still demonstrated elevated MI prevalence. • Hormone data: No information on hormone therapy exposure or duration was available.

Overall findings / implications

• Transgender adults showed elevated myocardial infarction risk independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors. • Risk appeared highest among transgender men, suggesting sex-specific or treatment-related vulnerabilities. • Findings highlight the need for enhanced cardiovascular risk assessment and prevention in transgender populations. • Lack of hormone exposure data limits causal inference and underscores the need for longitudinal, treatment-linked studies.

Physical health findings

• All-cause mortality: Overall mortality was higher than expected compared with the general population, particularly among transfeminine individuals. • Cardiovascular mortality: Increased cardiovascular-related deaths observed in transfeminine participants, especially those exposed to ethinyl estradiol. • Venous thromboembolism: Elevated mortality from VTE-related causes among transfeminine individuals; risk linked to older oestrogen formulations. • Cancer mortality: No overall increase in cancer-related mortality compared with the general population. • Transmasculine outcomes: Mortality rates among transmasculine participants were not significantly elevated. • Hormone exposure: Higher mortality risks were associated with long-term hormone use, particularly synthetic oestrogens.

Overall findings / implications

• Long-term hormone treatment, particularly older oestrogen regimens, was associated with increased cardiovascular and thromboembolic mortality in transfeminine individuals. • Findings support the transition away from ethinyl estradiol toward safer oestrogen formulations. • No evidence of increased cancer mortality provides reassurance regarding malignancy risk. • Results emphasise the importance of hormone choice, cardiovascular risk assessment, and long-term monitoring in gender-affirming endocrine care.

Physical health findings

• Cardiometabolic risk factors (≥45 years): Hypertension was the most prevalent risk factor (29%), followed by current smoking (24%), obesity (20%), dyslipidaemia (16%), and diabetes (9%). • Body mass index: Median BMI was 27.1 kg/m² (IQR 25.0–30.1), within the overweight range; individuals using transdermal estradiol had higher median BMI (29.6 kg/m²). • Hormone regimen and physiology: Serum estradiol concentrations did not differ significantly by age group (≥45 vs <45 years) or route of administration; sex steroid levels were within expected therapeutic ranges. • Route-specific patterns: Transdermal estradiol use was more common in individuals aged ≥45 years (31% vs 8%), while oral estradiol doses were lower in this age group. • Cardiovascular events: Prevalence of ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, and VTE was low in this cohort. • Laboratory measures: Routine clinical markers included BMI, blood pressure, lipids, glucose, SHBG, and serum estradiol.

Carmichael et al. (2021) Source
Also in: Mental HealthSocial Health
Quantitative (prospective uncontrolled observational study)To evaluate short-term physical, psychological and safety outcomes of GnRHa in 12–15-year-olds with persistent/severe GD.N=44; self-identified gender recorded (categories NR)
Extracted findings

Population

Youth

Age range (years)

12–15

Physical health findings

• Pubertal suppression: All participants achieved effective suppression of gonadotropins and sex steroids within 6 months, maintained throughout follow-up. • Bone health: No significant change in spine or hip BMD at 12 months; lumbar spine BMC and BMD increased at 24 months. Height-adjusted BMD z-scores declined during suppression but remained within expected ranges. • Growth and BMI: Height velocity slowed as expected; weight and BMI z-scores were stable to 24 months, with some increase by 36 months. • Menstrual and pubertal changes: All post-menarcheal participants became amenorrhoeic; no progression of pubertal development occurred. • Safety: Routine biochemistry and haematology remained normal; anticipated side effects (e.g. hot flushes, fatigue) were common but no serious adverse physical events were reported.

Overall findings / implications

Short-term pubertal suppression was physiologically effective and generally well tolerated in this selected cohort. • Bone density changes were consistent with suppression of pubertal progression, highlighting the need for ongoing bone health monitoring. • The absence of major short-term physical safety concerns supports cautious clinical use within specialist services. • Authors emphasise the need for larger, controlled, long-term studies to clarify longer-term physical outcomes, particularly skeletal health.

Reference

• Baseline somatic morbidity: Low and comparable between transgender individuals and controls (Charlson comorbidity index ≥1 in ~4–5%). • Cardiometabolic risk indicators: No excess baseline physical comorbidity detected prior to referral for gender-affirming care. • Hormone treatment exposure: Gender-affirming hormone therapy initiated in ~55% of the cohort, with median time to initiation 1–2 years post-diagnosis. • Surgical exposure: Gender-affirming surgery occurred in a minority; follow-up insufficient to assess post-surgical physical health outcomes. • Mortality/major physical outcomes: No signal of increased somatic mortality or severe physical disease identified within follow-up.

Overall findings / implications

• Physical health burden at baseline was low and comparable to the general population, suggesting no intrinsic excess somatic disease in transgender individuals entering care. • Observed health disparities in this cohort were driven primarily by mental health morbidity rather than physical illness. • Findings support the need to separate physical from mental health risk when interpreting outcomes in transgender populations. • Longer follow-up is required to assess long-term cardiometabolic and surgical outcomes associated with gender-affirming treatment.

Reference

Transmasculine vs cis women 1.75). • Cause-specific mortality: Significantly higher deaths from external causes (suicide, homicide, accidental poisoning), particularly compared with cisgender women (transfeminine MRR 1.92; transmasculine MRR 2.77). • Cancer mortality: Transfeminine adults had lower cancer mortality than cisgender women (MRR 0.52); no increased cancer mortality detected overall. • Endocrine causes: Higher mortality from endocrine, nutritional, and metabolic diseases compared with cisgender women (MRR 2.95). • Cardiovascular disease: No clear increase in CVD mortality detected, likely reflecting younger cohort age.

Physical health findings

• Baseline medical comorbidity: Overall rates of co-existing physical illness were low; most common conditions were dyslipidaemia (21.6%), asthma (11.5%), and hypertension (9.2%). • Cardiometabolic risk factors: 25% had elevated total cholesterol (>5.3 mmol/L) and 31% had elevated LDL (>2.6 mmol/L) at baseline; ~20% reported a family history of vascular disease. • Glucose metabolism: Elevated fasting glucose was uncommon; no confirmed diabetes on repeat testing. • Bone health: Among those undergoing DEXA (17.9% of cohort), 20.5% had osteopenia and 7.7% osteoporosis. • Hormone therapy exposure: 74.3% were receiving hormone therapy; 20.2% had used hormones prior to clinic presentation (including non-prescribed use). • Surgical interventions: 22.3% had undergone surgery; 9.2% had gender-affirming genital surgery. • Adverse physical effects: 17% reported adverse effects related to hormonal or surgical treatment (e.g. dyslipidaemia, hot flushes, headaches); serious complications were rare.

Overall findings / implications

• Physical health comorbidity was present but generally low in this relatively young adult cohort. • Cardiometabolic risk factors and bone health abnormalities were identified, supporting the need for routine screening prior to and during hormone therapy. • Adverse physical effects of treatment were uncommon and mostly mild, with low regret rates. • Findings support the importance of structured endocrine monitoring and integrated physical health care within gender services.

van Kesteren et al. (1997)Quantitative (Retrospective descriptive cohort study)To describe mortality and morbidity outcomes in trans people receiving GAHT.N=1,109; M→F, F→M transsexuals
Extracted findings

Population

Adult

Age range (years)

18–86

Physical health findings

• Mortality: Overall mortality in both transfeminine and transmasculine individuals was not increased compared with the general population. • Venous thromboembolism (VTE): Markedly increased incidence among transfeminine individuals using oral oestrogens (≈20-fold increase); risk was substantially lower with transdermal estradiol, particularly in those aged >40 years. • Cardiovascular disease: No increase in myocardial infarction mortality or morbidity compared with population expectations. • Cancer: No breast cancer cases observed; one prostate cancer case reported. Overall cancer mortality was not elevated. • Endocrine/liver effects: Frequent hyperprolactinaemia in transfeminine individuals, reversible with dose reduction; mild liver enzyme elevations occurred, usually transient. • Gallbladder disease: Slightly increased incidence of cholelithiasis, consistent with oestrogen exposure. • Transmasculine outcomes: No serious morbidity attributable to testosterone, aside from mild liver enzyme elevations and acne.

Overall findings / implications

Cross-sex hormone treatment was not associated with increased overall mortality when delivered under medical supervision. • VTE represents the most significant physical risk, particularly with older oral oestrogen regimens. • Findings strongly support the use of transdermal estradiol to reduce thrombotic risk in transfeminine individuals. • Results provide early evidence that gender-affirming hormone therapy can be physically safe, with appropriate regimen choice and monitoring. • Long-term surveillance remains important to identify rare or delayed adverse outcomes.

Reference

van Kesteren, P. J. M., Asscheman, H., Megens, J. A. J., & Gooren, L. J. G. (1997). Mortality and morbidity in transsexual subjects treated with cross-sex hormones. Clinical Endocrinology, 47(3), 337–342.

Physical health findings

• Hormone therapy exposure: 100% received clinician-prescribed GAHT; 31% had used hormones prior to clinic presentation, including 7.8% without medical supervision. • Thromboembolic events: 5 cases of DVT (2.1%) occurred over 1,380 patient-years, all in transfeminine individuals; most events occurred prior to clinic care or with older oestrogen regimens (ethinyl estradiol or conjugated equine oestrogens). • Current oestrogen safety: No DVT events were observed among patients treated with 17β-estradiol. • HIV prevalence: 6.6% of the cohort was HIV-positive; most had initiated hormones without medical supervision. • Surgical interventions: 31% of transfeminine and 64% of transmasculine participants accessed gender-affirming surgery; lack of insurance coverage limited surgical access. • General medical conditions: Low prevalence of documented chronic physical illness; no excess serious medical morbidity reported during follow-up.

• GAHT delivered within guideline-based endocrine care appeared physically safe, particularly with modern oestrogen formulations. • Thromboembolic risk was concentrated in unsupervised hormone use and older regimens, supporting structured medical oversight. • Limited insurance coverage constrained access to surgery, shaping physical health trajectories. • Findings reinforce the importance of early, supervised endocrine care to minimise preventable physical health risks.

Physical health findings

• Hormone regimens: MtF treated with 17β-estradiol plus anti-androgens; FtM treated with transdermal or intramuscular testosterone. • Thromboembolic/metabolic safety: No VTE events reported during the first year; lipid and glucose profiles largely stable, with pre-existing dyslipidaemia improving under monitoring. • Weight/BMI: Minimal weight change overall; 8.9% MtF and 18.5% FtM obese at 1 year. • Haematological effects: No anaemia (MtF) or polycythaemia (FtM); electrolytes remained normal with spironolactone. • Endocrine effects: Expected suppression of testosterone in MtF and physiological male-range testosterone in FtM; >20% MtF developed mild hyperprolactinaemia, without prolactinoma. • Other conditions: 3.6% cholelithiasis in MtF; isolated benign breast lesions; HIV-positive participants safely continued GAHT.

Physical health findings

• PCOS prevalence: 23.8% met criteria for PCOS, higher than estimates for the general adolescent population (8–13%). • Body mass index: Patients with PCOS had significantly higher BMI than those without PCOS (mean 33.1 vs 25.6 kg/m²). • Hyperandrogenism: PCOS group had higher total and free testosterone levels compared with non-PCOS peers. • Metabolic markers: Higher LDL cholesterol observed in the PCOS group; triglycerides and HDL did not differ significantly. • Glucose metabolism: Low prevalence of prediabetes (4.8%) and diabetes (0.9%); no significant difference by PCOS status. • Other endocrine conditions: No cases of CAH, Cushing’s disease, glucocorticoid resistance, or pregnancy were identified.

Overall findings / implications

• PCOS appears more prevalent among transmasculine adolescents than in the general population. • PCOS in this group clusters with obesity, hyperandrogenism, and dyslipidaemia, indicating early cardiometabolic risk. • GAHT initiation may mask PCOS features, highlighting the importance of early identification and baseline screening. • Findings support proactive metabolic and cardiovascular risk assessment and counselling in transmasculine youth presenting for care.

Reference

Rangi, S. K., Rehmer, J., & Ferrando, C. A. (2024). Prevalence of polycystic ovarian syndrome in young and adolescent transmasculine patients presenting for gender-affirming care. Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology, 37(1), 51–55. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpag.2023.09.003

(2017) SourceQuantitative (Retrospective cohort study using electronic health records from three large integrated healthcare systems, with matched cisgender comparison cohorts and longitudinal follow-up for incident cancer.)To estimate cancer incidence in transgender people enrolled in three integrated healthcare systems.N=4,889; transfeminine, transmasculine
Extracted findings

Population

Adult

Age range (years)

NR

Physical health findings

• Overall cancer incidence: No difference in all-cancer incidence for transfeminine (TF) or transmasculine (TM) participants compared with matched cisgender reference groups. • Transfeminine-specific risks: – Lower prostate cancer risk vs cisgender men (HR 0.4). – Higher endocrine gland cancer risk (HR 5.2) and viral infection–related cancers (HR 2.0) vs cisgender men. – Higher lymphatic/haematopoietic cancer risk vs cisgender women (HR 3.0). • Transmasculine-specific risks: – Higher breast cancer risk vs cisgender men, but no increase vs cisgender women. – Increased smoking- and viral-related cancers vs cisgender men, driven entirely by cervical cancer. • Hormone exposure: Cancer risks were observed in a cohort with access to healthcare; specific hormone dose/duration effects were not directly analysed. • Follow-up: Mean follow-up 4.0 years (TF) and 3.5 years (TM).

Overall findings / implications

• Cancer risk among transgender adults was largely comparable to cisgender populations when matched on age, race, and healthcare access. • Observed differences were site-specific and aligned with natal anatomy and screening practices rather than global cancer excess. • Findings support the importance of age- and anatomy-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. prostate, breast, cervical) in transgender care. • Longer follow-up is required to clarify lifetime cancer risk, particularly with prolonged hormone exposure.

Extracted findings

Physical health findings

• Weight status: Transgender students were more likely to be underweight (RR 4.78, 95% CI 1.61–14.18) and more likely to be obese (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.21–4.93) compared with non-transgender peers; no difference in overweight status. • Physical activity: Less likely to meet strenuous physical activity recommendations (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.01–1.34) and to engage in any strengthening activity (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.11–1.56). • Sedentary behaviour: More likely to exceed recommended screen time (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.02–1.41). • Dietary behaviours: No significant differences in fruit/vegetable intake, breakfast consumption, soda, fast food, or restaurant food consumption. • Body-related measures: No significant difference in unhealthy weight-control behaviours; body dissatisfaction slightly more common.

Overall findings / implications

• Transgender college students experience marked weight-related physical health disparities, with a bimodal pattern of underweight and obesity. • Lower physical activity and higher sedentary behaviour may contribute to long-term cardiometabolic risk. • Findings highlight the need for gender-affirming, inclusive physical activity and weight-related health interventions in college settings. • Structural barriers (e.g. safety and inclusion in recreational spaces) should be addressed to support healthier physical behaviours.

Physical health findings

• Overall somatic health: Adolescents seeking GAHT were generally physically healthy, with few chronic medical conditions. • Body mass index: 33% were overweight or obese (BMI > 25 kg/m²); overweight and obesity were more common in FtM adolescents than in the general adolescent population. • Respiratory and other conditions: Asthma (8%) was the most common physical condition; migraine and other chronic illnesses were rare. • Blood pressure: MtF adolescents had higher mean systolic BP than FtM adolescents, though values were largely within reference ranges. • Laboratory findings: Most baseline labs were within reference ranges; mild abnormalities included elevated LDL cholesterol and prolactin, particularly among those with prior non-prescribed hormone use. • Substance use: 14.5% reported regular smoking; no heavy alcohol or illicit drug use reported. • Contraindications: No absolute somatic contraindications to GAHT were identified.

• Adolescents seeking GAHT showed good baseline physical health, supporting the feasibility of medical intervention from a somatic perspective. • Overweight/obesity emerged as the main physical health concern, particularly among FtM youth, with early metabolic signals (e.g. HbA1c, ALT) in higher-BMI individuals. • Findings highlight the importance of routine physical screening and lifestyle counselling alongside gender-affirming care. • The absence of major somatic contraindications suggests that physical health rarely limits access to GAHT, though long-term follow-up is needed.

Physical health findings

• Baseline bone health: Low lumbar spine BMD present before GAHT in 21.9% of trans women and 4.3% of trans men (Z-score < –2.0). • Lumbar spine BMD: No significant change in absolute BMD over 10 years in trans women (+0.006 g/cm²) or trans men (+0.008 g/cm²). • Z-scores: Lumbar spine Z-scores increased over 10 years (trans women +0.22; trans men +0.34). • Hormone associations: – Higher estradiol levels associated with BMD increases in trans women. – Lower LH associated with BMD increases in trans men. • Hip/femoral neck: No significant changes detected (limited long-term data). • Monitoring tools: DXA scans; routine sex hormone blood tests.

Wiepjes et al. (2020) SourceQuantitative (Nationwide retrospective cohort study)To compare fracture incidence among trans people receiving long-term GAHT with an age-matched reference population.N=3,059; trans women (n=1,089 + 934), trans men (n=1,036)
Extracted findings

Physical health findings

• Fracture risk (trans women): – Overall fracture risk not increased compared with reference populations. – Higher fracture risk in trans women ≥50 years compared with age-matched cisgender men (OR 1.90), but similar to cisgender women. – Younger trans women showed a trend toward higher fracture risk vs cis women, but not vs cis men. • Fracture type: Trans women had a higher proportion of osteoporotic fractures (hip, spine, forearm, humerus) compared with cis men. • Bone density: Lower lumbar spine T-scores were associated with higher fracture risk; findings suggest low pre-treatment BMD rather than GAHT effects. • Trans men: No increased fracture risk; risk was lower than cis men and similar to cis women. • Hormone levels: Estradiol, testosterone, and LH levels were not independently associated with fracture risk.

Physical health findings

• Venous thromboembolism (VTE): 5.1% of trans women experienced VTE/PE during hormone therapy; nearly half occurred within the first year and several around gender-affirming surgery. Events were commonly associated with smoking, immobilisation, hypercholesterolaemia, or clotting disorders. • Cardiovascular disease: Trans women had higher prevalence of myocardial infarction than cisgender women, and higher cerebrovascular disease than cisgender men; rates were similar to cisgender men for MI. • Type 2 diabetes: Higher prevalence in both trans women and trans men compared with controls; many diagnoses pre-dated hormone therapy. • Obesity/BMI: BMI and obesity prevalence were similar to controls in both groups. • Cancer: No increased cancer prevalence compared with control populations; cancer types were heterogeneous and uncommon. • Trans men: No increase in MI, cerebrovascular disease, or VTE compared with controls; testosterone appeared relatively safe in the medium term.5.1% of trans women experienced VTE/PE during hormone therapy; nearly half occurred within the first year and several around gender-affirming surgery. Events were commonly associated with smoking, immobilisation, hypercholesterolaemia, or clotting disorders. • Cardiovascular disease: Trans women had higher prevalence of myocardial infarction than cisgender women, and higher cerebrovascular disease than cisgender men; rates were similar to cisgender men for MI. • Type 2 diabetes: Higher prevalence in both trans women and trans men compared with controls; many diagnoses pre-dated hormone therapy. • Obesity/BMI: BMI and obesity prevalence were similar to controls in both groups. • Cancer: No increased cancer prevalence compared with control populations; cancer types were heterogeneous and uncommon. • Trans men: No increase in MI, cerebrovascular disease, or VTE compared with controls; testosterone appeared relatively safe in the medium term.

Overall findings / implications

• Overall physical morbidity during gender-affirming hormone therapy was relatively low, particularly in trans men. • Trans women showed increased cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk, especially early in treatment and in the presence of modifiable risk factors. • Findings support careful cardiovascular risk assessment, smoking cessation, and regimen choice (route/type of oestrogen) in trans women. • Cancer risk was not elevated, providing reassurance regarding medium-term malignancy outcomes. • Results reinforce the importance of individualised risk management and long-term monitoring during hormone therapy.

Wierckx et al. (2014) SourceQuantitative (prospective multicentre cohort; 1-year follow-up)To describe short-term hormonal/clinical changes, side effects and adverse events during GAHT in trans men and trans women.N=106; trans men (n=53), trans women (n=53)
Extracted findings

Population

Adult

Age range (years)

NR

Physical health findings

• Serious adverse events: No deaths, cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, or osteoporotic fractures observed during 12-month follow-up. • Trans men (testosterone): – Increased lean mass, decreased fat mass, and shift to android fat distribution. – Modest increases in LDL-C, total cholesterol, triglycerides; HDL-C decreased. – Hematocrit increased; erythrocytosis occurred in ~4%. – Mild liver enzyme elevations common; clinically significant abnormalities rare. • Trans women (oestrogen + antiandrogen): – Increased fat mass, reduced lean mass, gynoid fat redistribution. – Decreases in total cholesterol and LDL-C; HDL-C also decreased. – Fasting insulin increased, but no cases of diabetes. – Prolactin increased, especially with cyproterone acetate; symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia rare. • Blood pressure: Small increases observed, but no new hypertension diagnoses.

Overall findings / implications

• Contemporary GAHT regimens were effective and physically safe in the short term, with a low rate of clinically significant adverse events. • Observed metabolic and body-composition changes were expected and sex-steroid related, supporting the biological plausibility of findings. • Results reinforce the importance of routine metabolic, hematologic, and liver monitoring, particularly during the first year of treatment. • Findings support the continued use of modern oestrogen formulations and dosing strategies to minimise cardiovascular and thrombotic risk.

Data are the review team's extraction tables (Supplementary File S2, version dated 30 September 2026). Author–year labels correspond to entries in the manuscript reference list. Sample sizes are as reported by the original studies; where a study reports a total and an analytic sub-sample, both are given.

Findings summarise what each study reported and are not a re-analysis. For any figure used in citation, consult the original paper via the Source link.
